known: Item.owner_id is declared as a foreign key without index=True (backend/app/models.py:97) and no migration creates an index on item.owner_id (the only create_index in migrations is ix_user_email).
The container starts 4 worker processes (backend/Dockerfile CMD).
All route handlers except health_check are sync def; the database engine is created with create_engine defaults and no pool arguments (backend/app/core/db.py:6).
The DB session is opened per request by a dependency and held for the whole request (backend/app/api/deps.py:21-23).
unknown: Rows in item and user tables
assumed: The item table grows with users over time; no sizing evidence either way.
derived: Connections upper bound per host = 4 workers x per-process pool size; the pool size is the library default and is not stated in the repository, so no number is asserted.

root_causes.description: The items listing filters and sorts on columns with no supporting index.
Slow external or CPU-heavy work runs inline in a request while holding a pooled database session and a worker thread.
List endpoints accept an unbounded client-controlled page size.

findings.problem: GET /items/ runs a count(*) and a filtered, ordered, paginated select on item.owner_id, but item.owner_id has no index and there is no composite index supporting the ORDER BY created_at.
findings.performance_principle: Work per request should be proportional to the result, not to the size of the whole data set; selective filters need an access path that avoids scanning everything.

evidence.statement: Non-superuser branch filters both the count and the page query on Item.owner_id and orders by created_at desc with offset/limit.
owner_id is a foreign key with no index=True.

No migration creates an index on item; the only create_index is ix_user_email. PostgreSQL does not index referencing columns of foreign keys automatically (general database fact, not shown in the repo).
No runtime evidence (no EXPLAIN, no metrics) is committed; the cost depends on table size.

findings.conditions: Matters once the item table is large enough that a sequential scan is measurably slower than an index lookup (workload unknown; the size at which this happens is an assumption, not read from the repo). Also affects the cascade DELETE of a user's items in delete_user and the ON DELETE CASCADE foreign key checks, which probe item.owner_id.

counter_evidence.statement: Small tables are scanned quickly and the planner may choose a seq scan regardless; impact is bounded when item counts are small.
Searched for any index on item (op.create_index, index=True, Index(...)) and found none.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: The template is a starter; if each deployment holds a few thousand items total, a sequential scan is cheap and the index adds write overhead for no visible gain.
findings.recommendation: Add a migration creating a btree index on item(owner_id, created_at DESC) (or at least owner_id); consider an index on created_at separately if superusers list all items often. This removes the full scan for the filter, count and sort rather than hiding it.

alternatives.why: Fixes the filter and the cascade, but the ORDER BY created_at still requires sorting the owner's rows.
Serves filter, sort and the count for the owner.

alternatives.option: Cache the count or drop it
alternatives.why: Adds invalidation or an API change and does not fix the page query.

findings.trade_offs: Extra index storage and slightly slower inserts/updates of item; a migration on a large table should be built concurrently to avoid long write locks.

validation.metric: Plan node type and execution time of the items list and count queries for a representative owner
validation.expectation: Plan changes from Seq Scan on item to an index scan; rows examined fall to the owner's row count.
validation.falsifier: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a realistically sized table already shows an acceptable plan, with no measurable difference after the index.
validation.guard: A test or migration check asserting an index covering item.owner_id exists.

commands.command: psql -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM item WHERE owner_id = '<uuid>' ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET 0 LIMIT 100"
commands.purpose: Show the current plan for the list query on a staging copy.

commands.command: psql -c "SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'item'"
commands.purpose: Confirm which indexes exist on item.

findings.problem: SMTP delivery runs synchronously inside the request handler (password recovery, user creation, test email) while the request's database session is still open and the handler occupies a worker thread; the repository sets no SMTP timeout.
findings.performance_principle: Slow external I/O on the request path couples request latency and shared-resource hold time to a dependency's tail latency; work the caller does not need to wait for should be decoupled.

evidence.statement: recover_password calls send_email inline after a DB lookup; the response waits for delivery.
send_email builds smtp_options with host, port, tls, user and password only; no timeout option is set, and message.send is a blocking call.
The Session from get_db is held until the response completes (yield dependency), so a pooled connection is retained during SMTP.
The same inline pattern appears in create_user (users.py:73) and test_email (utils.py:21).

findings.conditions: Assumes email is enabled in production and the SMTP provider is slow or unreachable at some point; password-recovery is unauthenticated, so the request rate to it is client-controlled. Whether the emails library applies its own default socket timeout is not determined here.

counter_evidence.statement: Endpoint is low-traffic by nature, and a healthy SMTP server answers quickly; the handler is sync def so it runs in a threadpool and does not block the event loop.
Recovery is only sent when the user exists, so the unauthenticated slow path is limited to known addresses.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If email is disabled or the provider is fast and reliable, and traffic to these endpoints is low, the inline send is harmless.
findings.recommendation: Set an explicit SMTP timeout and move sending to FastAPI BackgroundTasks (or a queue if delivery guarantees are needed) so the request returns after the token is created.

alternatives.why: No new infrastructure; removes SMTP from the response latency.
Bounds the worst case but still holds the request open for the full send.
More durable but adds operational burden not justified without volume evidence.

findings.trade_offs: Background sends lose the ability to return a delivery error to the caller and are lost on process crash unless a queue is used; the recovery endpoint already hides failures by design.

validation.metric: p95 latency of POST /password-recovery/{email} with SMTP host delayed, and time the DB connection is checked out
validation.expectation: Latency becomes independent of SMTP latency after the change.
validation.falsifier: Latency with a delayed SMTP stub is unchanged after the change, or the emails library already enforces a short timeout and the delay never materialises.
validation.guard: Test with a stub SMTP server that sleeps, asserting the endpoint returns promptly.

findings.problem: List endpoints (users and items) take client-supplied skip and limit with no upper bound, run an extra count(*) every call, and materialise and validate every row into Pydantic models; a large limit returns the whole table in one response.
findings.performance_principle: Per-request work and memory should be bounded by the server, not by caller input.

evidence.statement: limit: int = 100 with no maximum, skip with no maximum.
Same for items; rows are converted with a list comprehension of model_validate and returned as one response.

findings.conditions: Only matters if a caller requests a very large limit against a large table; users listing is superuser-only and items listing is scoped to the caller unless superuser. Deep skip offsets also scan skipped rows.

counter_evidence.statement: Both users listing (superuser) and normal items listing (own rows) are access-limited, which bounds who can trigger it.

findings.recommendation: Constrain with Query(100, ge=1, le=<server maximum>) and skip ge=0; consider keyset pagination if deep paging is expected.
findings.trade_offs: Clients that currently request more than the cap will need to page; this is an API behaviour change.

validation.metric: Response size and handler time for a very large limit on a large table
validation.expectation: Requests above the cap are rejected or clamped, bounding memory per request.
validation.falsifier: Table sizes remain small enough that no request can return a material payload.

findings.problem: Login hashes with memory-hard Argon2 inside a sync handler while holding a DB session; unknown emails also pay a full dummy verification, so every login attempt (valid or not) costs a full hash and an unauthenticated caller controls the rate.
findings.performance_principle: CPU- and memory-heavy work on a shared, bounded worker pool saturates it linearly with request rate; such work should be rate-limited and kept out of resource-holding scopes.

evidence.statement: authenticate verifies the password on both the found and not-found branch (dummy hash) inside the open session.
DUMMY_HASH records Argon2 parameters m=65536,t=3,p=4 (a 64 MiB memory cost per verification as encoded in the hash string).
login_access_token is a sync def that opens a pooled session via dependency; the deployment runs 4 worker processes; no rate limiting or login throttling exists in the repo.
Password change and user create/update/signup hash on the same path (users.py:110-114, crud.py:13, crud.py:26).

findings.conditions: Matters under concurrent logins or a credential-stuffing burst against /login/access-token; no figures for login rate or container CPU/memory limits are available, so cost per hash is not asserted. Mitigated only if an upstream proxy rate limits.

counter_evidence.statement: Cost is deliberate for password security and sync handlers run in a threadpool so the event loop stays free; normal login traffic is low relative to other endpoints.
No rate limiter found in app code or Traefik labels in compose.yml.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Hashing cost is a security trade-off; for an app with low login volume and a rate-limiting proxy in front, this is working as intended.
findings.recommendation: Do not weaken the hash. Release the DB session before hashing (read the user, close, then verify), and add login rate limiting at the proxy or app level; size worker memory for concurrent hashes.

alternatives.why: Bounds hash work from unauthenticated callers without lowering security.
Trades security for throughput; not justified without measurements.

findings.trade_offs: Rate limiting can lock out legitimate users behind shared IPs; releasing the session early needs a small restructure of the dependency lifetime.

validation.metric: Login p95 latency, worker CPU and RSS, and checked-out pool connections under N concurrent POST /login/access-token
validation.expectation: After rate limiting, saturation under attack traffic is bounded; pool occupancy during hashing drops if the session is released first.
validation.falsifier: A load test at realistic concurrency shows flat latency and memory, indicating hashing is not a bottleneck at expected load.
validation.guard: Alert on login latency and 4xx rate on the token endpoint.

considered_not_reported.observation: Default SQLAlchemy engine pool (no pool_size, pool_recycle or pool_pre_ping set) with 4 workers.
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Defaults are reasonable for this request profile; no evidence of exhaustion and the bound depends on unknown Postgres max_connections.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Pool timeout errors appear or replicas are scaled so workers x pool size approaches max_connections.

considered_not_reported.observation: get_current_user does one session.get(User) per authenticated request.
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Primary-key lookup, one query, bounded and standard; no evidence it is a bottleneck.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Profiling shows the user lookup dominating cheap endpoints.

considered_not_reported.observation: Sentry enable_tracing=True with default sample behaviour.
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Sampling rate and DSN presence are deployment-specific; nothing evidences overhead.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Sentry is enabled in production and tracing overhead is measured.
